method: eye diameter along the dorsal-ventral midline measured with digital callipers (specimens under 10 mm mantle length) or a standard ruler (larger specimens), on preserved museum specimens (the paper states fixation in 5% buffered formalin and storage in 70–80% ethanol only for the seven specimens taken for histology)
conditions: Range over the specimens with intact eyes, not an adult value and not a species maximum: the sentence gives 0.5 to 33 mm eye diameter for mantle lengths 1.5 to 165 mm among specimens with intact eyes. Specimens were loaned from NIWA and the National Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa; capture depths known, day or night not recorded; preservation is stated only for the seven histology specimens (5% buffered formalin, then 70–80% ethanol), and the paper does not mention shrinkage or any correction for it. Verbatim on the page (audit 445): 87 specimens of 1.5 to 210 mm ML, 30 adults (23 reproductively mature or mated), 61 with eyes intact enough to measure, eye about 1:5 of ML across development (log-log R2 = 0.929; tighter below ML 50 mm, n = 33, than above, n = 28). Sexes not given in the text read. The largest intact eye (33 mm) therefore comes from a specimen of at most 165 mm ML.

value: with the light-organ dummy (glow stick) present, spent significantly more time, 30.22 +/- 1.8% (SEM), in the centre of the cave
method: in situ night-time video of wild fish at their reef cave entrances; dummies placed in the cave centre (approximately 1 m diameter, periphery approximately 2 m): a 100 mm painted fish dummy with glow-stick light organs, a 500 nm LED blinking at 1 Hz, and a constant glow stick (4.5 mm diameter, 37 mm long, 519 nm peak, light surface reduced to 10 mm)
conditions: Wild fish, Dahab (Gulf of Aqaba, Red Sea), night; sex and age not determined (sex only guessed from body length, 4-7 cm potential males, 7-10 cm potential females); N = 8 fish confronted with the glow stick (11 with the fish dummy, 6 with the LED; verbatim, audit 445). Territorial aggression is the response measured. Figure 2D compares blank (no dummy), fish-dummy, blinking-LED and glow-stick recordings (one-way ANOVA with Holm-Sidak post hoc); the paper describes no unlit or non-luminous dummy, so the extra time in the centre is not assigned to the light rather than to an object placed there, although the differing responses to the three luminous dummies show the fish distinguishes them. Every stimulus was recorded for 5 min in sequential sessions; stimulus order and randomisation are not stated. Colour discrimination was not tested: the authors write 'Therefore, we assume no wavelength dependent effects in behavior by using a 500 nm LED and a 519 nm glow stick.' after preliminary observations that small constant green, blue and red lights all drew approach (Methods; not a quoted value). The wavelengths of the dummies differ (519 nm glow stick, 500 nm LED) and shape, size and blinking differ across dummies, so dummy types are not matched on intensity; whether each fish was tested once, whether fish were independent animals, and the comparison used for 'significantly more' were not read. Verbatim on the page (audit 445): undisturbed fish spent 98.32% +/- 0.77 SEM of time in the periphery; with the blinking LED fish spent 95.28 +/- 0.14% in the periphery and with the fish dummy 89.47% (the page prints this with an apparent typo, so the fish-dummy figure is not carried as a value). Non-visual cues from the glow stick (chemical) were not ruled out in the text read.
